correctness.rationale: Walsh eigenvalue identities are derived for each distance shell with exact undirected-edge normalization. Strict convexity verifies all critical ratios. Parseval and the derivative influence inequality reduce every relevant ground state to at most four input coordinates. The complete 65536-function four-variable truth-table census and the separate constructive classifications establish all finite low-degree counts; exhaustive Q4 spin calculations independently agree at five coupling choices. No sample-based extrapolation is used for the all-dimensional conclusion.

originality.rationale: Comparisons considered the physical two-range interaction model, all-dimensional Fourier-degree reduction, and exact class counts rather than matching titles. Kalz et al. concern a square lattice; Nisan-Szegedy establish degree/influence methods but no hypercube spin multiplet; Jovanovski treats ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor-only dynamics. No inspected accessible result gives the coupled threshold and quartic coexistence theorem. An unindexed direct enumeration remains a priority risk.
residual_risks: Published record full files were not accessible; indexed synopsis alone does not establish an exhaustive absence of related counts.
Unindexed physical Hamiltonian tables and Boolean-degree-two censuses could already imply some numbers.

The broad spectral energy formula alone is an immediate Hamming-scheme diagonalization; mathematical novelty is assessed in the exact low-degree ground-state multiplicity classification, not the spectral identity in isolation.

value.rationale: An exact two-range antiferromagnetic hypercube provides a natural finite frustrated-spin benchmark. At the second zero-temperature coupling crossing its labeled degeneracy is quartic in dimension with genuinely four-coordinate families, revealing nontrivial coexistence missing from the simple Walsh energy minimization. The dimension-uniform exact sector counts are motivated physical observables and are not arbitrary numerical slices or a claim of thermodynamic criticality.
